lessons.title: The Indian Compliance Layer: Private Placement, Valuation Reports, FEMA Filings and Angel Tax

children.text: In a Delaware seed round the founder signs, the wire arrives and the cap table updates. In India, the same transaction passes through company law, valuation rules, foreign exchange regulations and income tax, each with its own forms and deadlines. None of it is optional, the penalties are real, and the work usually lands on a founder who has never heard of most of it. This lesson maps the layer so you know what your company secretary is doing and what happens if nobody does it.

body.text: Indian fundraising has a rule that surprises every first-time founder: money in your bank account is not yet yours to spend. Until shares are allotted and the return is filed, the investor's money sits in a separate account, doing nothing.

children.text: Private Placement: How Indian Companies Legally Issue Shares

markDefs.definition: An offer of securities to a selected group of identified people, rather than to the public. It is the route through which almost every Indian startup round is issued.

children.text: A private limited company cannot invite the public to buy shares, so funding rounds go through the
route under the Companies Act, 2013. The mechanics are prescriptive, and each step has a form and a deadline attached.

events.title: Valuation report
events.description: A report from a registered valuer supports the price at which shares are being issued. Where a foreign investor is involved, a separate pricing certificate is also needed.

events.title: Board and shareholder approvals
events.description: The board approves the offer, and shareholders pass a special resolution authorising the private placement.

events.title: Offer letter to identified investors
events.description: A private placement offer letter in the prescribed form goes to the named investors only. The offer cannot be advertised or made generally available.

events.title: Money received through banking channels
events.description: Funds come by cheque, demand draft or electronic transfer from the investor's own account into a separate bank account. Cash is not permitted.

events.title: Allotment within 60 days
events.description: The board allots shares within 60 days of receiving the money. Miss it and the money must be refunded, with interest if the refund is also delayed.

events.title: Return of allotment filed
events.description: The company files the return of allotment with the Registrar within the prescribed period. Only after this filing can the money be used.

events.title: Certificates and registers
events.description: Share certificates are issued and the register of members updated, so the cap table and the statutory records match.

body.text: Three rules founders break most often: spending the money before allotment and filing, accepting subscription money from an account that is not the investor's own, and treating the 60-day allotment window as flexible. The penalties under the private placement provisions are severe, running into crores, and they attach to the company and its officers.

body.title: The deadline that catches people out
body.prompt: A startup receives ₹4 crore of subscription money into its separate bank account on 10 April. Within how many days of receiving that money must the board allot shares?
body.explanation: Allotment must happen within 60 days of receipt. If it does not, the company has to refund the money within a short prescribed window, and interest becomes payable if even that refund is late. Investors' lawyers track this date closely, so put it in your calendar the day the money lands.

children.text: Founders are often confused about why their company secretary asks for more than one valuation. The reason is that different laws ask the question for different purposes, and each prescribes who may answer it.

body.caption: Which valuation is needed, and why

cells: Company law valuation
To support the price at which new shares are issued under the private placement route
A registered valuer
Foreign exchange pricing certificate
To confirm a non-resident is not paying below fair value, under the pricing guidelines
A chartered accountant, merchant banker or practising cost accountant
Income tax valuation
To establish fair market value of unquoted shares under the income tax valuation rules
A merchant banker, under the prescribed method
ESOP and perquisite valuation
To compute the taxable value when employees exercise options
A merchant banker, at the time of exercise

body.label: The valuation report is not the negotiation
body.value: It supports the price, it does not set it
body.context: Your round price comes from negotiation, as Lesson 3.2 showed. The valuation report exists so that regulators and the tax authority can see the price was not arbitrary. Problems arise when the negotiated price and the supportable valuation are far apart.

children.text: Foreign money brings a second rulebook, administered by the Reserve Bank of India through authorised dealer banks. Most startup sectors allow foreign investment freely, without prior approval, but the reporting is mandatory and time-bound.

stats.label: Entity registration
stats.context: Done once, through your authorised dealer bank, before any filing

stats.label: Reporting an issue of shares
stats.context: The standard reporting form for foreign investment into the company

stats.label: Reporting a transfer
stats.context: Applies when shares move between a resident and a non-resident

stats.label: Late filing
stats.context: Delays are regularisable, but they cost money and slow your next round's diligence

body.text: One rule catches founders by surprise: investment from entities of countries sharing a land border with India requires prior government approval, including where the beneficial owner is located in such a country. Check the ultimate ownership of any foreign investor, not just the entity signing the cheque. A structure that looks Singaporean can still fall inside this rule.

body.label: RBI FIRMS portal
body.description: The Reserve Bank's single master form portal, where entity registration and foreign investment reporting are filed through your authorised dealer bank.

children.text: Angel Tax: What It Was, and Where It Stands

For over a decade, the single most feared line in Indian startup finance was angel tax. It worked in a way that felt absurd to founders: if a company issued shares above their computed fair market value, the excess premium was treated as income of the company and taxed. Raise ₹5 crore at a valuation the tax officer thought was too optimistic, and the company could receive a demand on the difference.

body.title: The angel tax timeline, and why it still matters

children.text: The provision was introduced as Section 56(2)(viib) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, applying to share premium received from resident investors above fair market value. Its history shaped how Indian rounds are documented to this day.

Aimed at money laundering through inflated share premiums, it caught genuine startups instead, because early-stage valuations are inherently forward-looking and no valuation model justifies them to a sceptical assessing officer.
DPIIT-recognised startups could claim an exemption, subject to conditions on size and investor type, which is one of the practical reasons founders sought recognition.
In 2023 the scope was widened to cover premium received from non-resident investors as well, which alarmed the venture industry considerably.
The provision was then abolished for all classes of investors with effect from assessment year 2025-26, announced in the Union Budget of July 2024 and widely welcomed by founders and funds.

Why it still matters. Assessments for earlier years can remain open, so older rounds can still attract questions. The habit of supporting every round with a defensible valuation report has stayed, and rightly so. And other provisions taxing shares issued or transferred below fair value continue to exist, so pricing still has tax consequences. Since India has also moved to new income tax legislation, confirm the current position and section references with a tax adviser rather than relying on any summary, including this one.

body.title: Can the money be spent?
body.question: A startup receives ₹6 crore of subscription money into a separate bank account on 2 June. The board has not yet allotted shares. The founders want to pay June salaries from it. What is the correct position?
options: Yes, the money belongs to the company once it is received
Yes, provided the allotment happens within 60 days
No, subscription money cannot be used until shares are allotted and the return of allotment is filed
No, unless the investor gives written permission
body.explanation: Under the private placement rules, subscription money must sit in a separate bank account and cannot be utilised until the shares are allotted and the return of allotment is filed with the Registrar. Paying salaries out of it early is a breach, however commercially sensible it feels.

body.title: A foreign cheque with a complication
body.scenario: Ruchi's Pune robotics startup has a ₹28 crore Series A led by a Singapore-incorporated fund. During diligence her lawyer notices two things. First, one of the fund's significant beneficial owners is resident in a country sharing a land border with India. Second, the company's previous round, raised from a US angel two years ago, was allotted on time but the foreign investment reporting was never filed.
body.prompt: What does each issue mean for this round, and what should she do?
body.modelAnswer:
Issue one: the land border rule. Investment from entities of countries sharing a land border with India, including cases where the beneficial owner sits in such a country, needs prior government approval. This is not a filing you catch up on later, it is a gate before the investment. Ruchi should get formal written confirmation of the fund's beneficial ownership structure, take specialist advice immediately, and if the rule applies, either route the round through the approval process, which takes months, or restructure the syndicate so the round can close from investors who are not caught. Either way she must tell the lead now and re-plan the runway, because a three-month delay changes her cash position.
Issue two: the unfiled reporting on the previous round. An unreported foreign investment is a regularisable default. The fix is to file the delayed report through the authorised dealer bank with the applicable late submission fee, and to disclose it in the disclosure letter. It will not usually kill a deal, but it will sit as a condition precedent and every future diligence will find it, so clear it now rather than at the next round.
The general lesson: foreign investment compliance is not paperwork you attend to after closing. The land border rule can stop a round entirely, and unfiled reports compound quietly until somebody looks.

body.caption: Who does what in a typical round

cells: Company secretary
Board and shareholder resolutions, offer letter, allotment, Registrar filings, statutory registers
Registered valuer or merchant banker
Valuation reports and pricing certificates for company law, foreign exchange and tax purposes
Authorised dealer bank
Entity registration and submission of foreign investment reporting on the RBI portal
Chartered accountant
Accounting treatment, statutory dues, tax positions and the tax implications of pricing
Lawyer
Definitive agreements, amended Articles, conditions precedent and the disclosure letter
Founder
Knowing every deadline exists, and chasing the people above until each one is met

body.text: Compliance failures rarely cause damage on the day they happen. They surface at the next round, when an investor's lawyer builds a list of defaults and turns each one into a condition precedent, a price adjustment or an indemnity. A clean compliance history is quietly worth money at every future raise.

body.title: Round closing compliance pack
steps: Valuation report obtained before the offer letter is issued, not afterwards.
Board resolution and shareholders' special resolution passed and minuted.
Private placement offer letter sent only to the identified investors, with the record maintained.
Separate bank account opened, and all subscription money received from each investor's own account through banking channels.
Allotment completed within the prescribed window from receipt of money.
Return of allotment filed with the Registrar, and only then the funds utilised.
Share certificates issued and the register of members updated.
Where any investor is non-resident: entity registration done, pricing certificate obtained, and the investment reported within the prescribed period.
Beneficial ownership of every foreign investor checked against the land border approval requirement.
Stamp duty on issue of securities paid, and the whole pack saved in the data room for the next round.

body.title: The money that is not yours yet
body.textWithBlank: Subscription money received under a private placement must be kept in a ___ bank account and cannot be used until shares are allotted and the return of allotment is filed.
body.explanation: The separate account requirement exists so that subscription money can be traced and refunded if the allotment does not happen. Spending from it early is one of the most common and most serious breaches by first-time founders.

cards.definition: An offer of shares to identified persons rather than the public, the route used for Indian startup rounds.
A shareholder approval requiring a high majority of votes cast, needed to authorise a private placement.
The filing with the Registrar recording newly allotted shares. Funds cannot be used until it is filed.
A professional registered to issue valuation reports supporting the price of newly issued shares.
Foreign exchange rules requiring that a non-resident does not acquire shares below fair value.
The fee payable to regularise a delayed foreign investment filing.
The former provision taxing share premium above fair market value as company income, abolished for all investors from assessment year 2025-26.

points: Indian rounds are issued through the private placement route, which prescribes approvals, an offer letter to identified investors, banking channels and strict deadlines.
Subscription money sits in a separate account and cannot be spent until shares are allotted and the return of allotment is filed.
Allotment must happen within 60 days of receiving the money, failing which it must be refunded, with interest if the refund is late.
Different laws demand different valuations: company law, foreign exchange pricing and income tax each prescribe who may certify.
The valuation report supports a negotiated price, it does not set it.
Foreign investment brings entity registration, a pricing certificate and time-bound reporting, with late submission fees for delays.
Investment linked to countries sharing a land border with India needs prior government approval, including through beneficial ownership.
Angel tax was abolished for all investors from assessment year 2025-26, but earlier years can still be assessed and defensible valuations remain essential.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. Company law procedures, foreign exchange reporting requirements, valuation rules and income tax provisions change frequently, and India has moved to new income tax legislation, so section references and timelines must be verified against current law. Always work with a qualified company secretary, chartered accountant and lawyer on any funding round. Ruchi's company and all figures are illustrative.
